summary: On a Sabbath Jesus gives sight to a man born blind; the Pharisees throw the man out, but Jesus finds him, and he believes and worships.
key_insight: The man’s sight grows step by step: “A Man called Jesus” (v. 11), “He is a prophet” (v. 17), a Man “from God” (v. 33), and at last, “Lord, I believe!” (v. 38). The Pharisees move the other way, from questions to the certainty that “this Man is a sinner.”
story: As Jesus passed by in Jerusalem, He saw a man who had been blind from birth. His disciples asked, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but that the works of God should be revealed in him.” He must do the works of the One who sent Him while it was day. “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”
Then He spat on the ground, made clay with the saliva, and anointed the blind man’s eyes. “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam,” He said. Siloam means Sent. The man went and washed, and came back seeing.

His neighbors argued over him. “Is not this he who sat and begged?” Some said yes; others said he only looked like him. He kept saying, “I am he.” Asked how his eyes were opened, he told them simply: “A Man called Jesus made clay and anointed my eyes.” Where was Jesus now? He did not know.

They brought him to the Pharisees, for it was a Sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Some of the Pharisees said, “This Man is not from God, because He does not keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” Divided, they asked the man what he thought. “He is a prophet,” he said.

The leaders would not believe he had been blind until they called his parents. The parents said this was their son and that he had been born blind, but they would say nothing about how he could now see, because anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. “He is of age; ask him.”

So they called the man a second time. “Give God the glory! We know that this Man is a sinner.” He answered, “Whether He is a sinner or not I do not know. One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see.” When they pressed him again, he asked whether they too wanted to become His disciples. They reviled him: “You are His disciple, but we are Moses’ disciples.” He would not give way: “If this Man were not from God, He could do nothing.” They answered, “You were completely born in sins, and are you teaching us?” And they cast him out.

Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and He found him. “Do you believe in the Son of God?” The man answered, “Who is He, Lord, that I may believe in Him?” Jesus said, “You have both seen Him and it is He who is talking with you.” He said, “Lord, I believe!” And he worshiped Him.

Jesus said, “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may be made blind.” Some Pharisees nearby asked, “Are we blind also?” Jesus answered, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains.”

scene.label: “Who sinned?”
scene.text: Many assumed that suffering came as punishment for a particular sin, as Job’s friends did. Jesus does not deny that sin brought suffering into the world, but He refuses to trace this man’s blindness to anyone’s sin.

scene.label: The pool of Siloam
scene.text: Siloam lay at the south end of the city, fed by the tunnel King Hezekiah cut from the Gihon spring (2 Kings 20:20). In 2004 workers uncovered a large stepped pool there from Jesus’ time. John translates the name, “Sent,” a word he often uses of Jesus (9:4).

scene.label: Clay on the Sabbath
scene.text: Jewish teaching, later written down in the Mishnah, listed kneading among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath. Making clay, and healing a man whose life was not in danger, both crossed the lines the Pharisees drew.

scene.label: Out of the synagogue
scene.text: Being put out of the synagogue meant being cut off from worship and from the life of the community. Jesus later warned His disciples that the same would happen to them (John 16:2).

scene.label: “Give God the glory!”
scene.text: This was a solemn call to tell the truth, as when Joshua urged Achan to “give glory to the LORD God of Israel” and confess (Joshua 7:19). The leaders meant: admit that this Man is a sinner.

witnesses.john: Only John records this sign. It acts out Jesus’ words, “I am the light of the world” (8:12; 9:5), and John tells it like a trial: the healed man becomes Jesus’ witness, while his judges show their own blindness. The other Gospels record Jesus healing blind men, but only John records one blind from birth.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the light of the world who opens eyes no one had ever opened. And when the man is thrown out for telling the truth about Him, Jesus goes looking for him.
seeing.living: The man did not have every answer, but he told what he knew: “One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see.” Tell plainly what Jesus has done for you, even when it costs you standing with people you respect. If it does, He will find you.
seeing.ponder: Where might you be saying, like the Pharisees, “We see,” when Jesus wants to open your eyes?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus opens the eyes of the blind and finds the outcast, but those sure they see stay blind.
outline: A blind man and a question about sin (1–7)
A witness who would not back down (8–34)
preaching.watch_for: The chapter is built like a trial: neighbors, Pharisees, parents and the man are all questioned, and the word “know” keeps returning (vv. 12, 20–21, 24–25, 29–31). By the end, the judges are the ones on trial (vv. 39–41).
